claim: PRIME generates cell-specific genome-scale metabolic models (GSMMs) based on molecular and phenotypic data.
source: To this end we present an approach termed PRIME for generating cell-specific genome-scale metabolic models (GSMMs) based on molecular and phenotypic data.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that PRIME generates cell-specific GSMMs using molecular and phenotypic data as inputs.

claim: More than 280 models of normal and cancer cell-lines were built using PRIME.
source: We build >280 models of normal and cancer cell-lines that successfully predict metabolic phenotypes in an individual manner.
evidence: The abstract states the number of models built and their predictive success.

claim: PRIME-derived models successfully predict metabolic phenotypes in an individual manner.
source: We build >280 models of normal and cancer cell-lines that successfully predict metabolic phenotypes in an individual manner.
evidence: The abstract claims successful prediction of metabolic phenotypes, which is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MLYCD is predicted as a top drug target that selectively inhibits cancerous but not normal cell proliferation.
source: The top predicted target, MLYCD, is experimentally validated and the metabolic effects of MLYCD depletion investigated.
evidence: The abstract states MLYCD as the top predicted target with experimental validation.

claim: MLYCD depletion was experimentally validated to selectively inhibit cancer cell proliferation.
source: The top predicted target, MLYCD, is experimentally validated and the metabolic effects of MLYCD depletion investigated.
evidence: The abstract explicitly mentions experimental validation of MLYCD as a selective target.

claim: PRIME successfully inferred the prognosis of cancer patients based on their individual GSMMs.
source: Furthermore, we tested cell-specific predicted responses to the inhibition of metabolic enzymes, and successfully inferred the prognosis of cancer patients based on their PRIME-derived individual GSMMs.
evidence: The abstract states successful inference of patient prognosis using PRIME models.

claim: Personalized medicine can facilitate the use of highly tailored therapies in cancer treatment.
source: The use of molecular data to personalize cancer treatment and differentiate one type of cancer from another can facilitate the use of highly tailored therapies and offers tremendous potential for improved prognoses (Simon and Roychowdhury, 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference supporting the potential of personalized medicine in cancer therapy.

claim: Two Genome-Scale Metabolic Models (GSMMs) of human metabolism were published in recent years.
source: In recent years, two Genome-Scale Metabolic Models (GSMMs) of human metabolism were published (Duarte et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2007), and their utility in predicting human metabolic phenotypes has been demonstrated in a wide range of studies (Shlomi et al., 2008; Lewis et al., 2010; Folger et al., 2011; Frezza et al., 2011; Agren et al., 2012; Yizhak et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites specific publications of human GSMMs.

claim: More comprehensive versions of the generic human metabolic model were published.
source: Recently, more comprehensive versions of the generic human model were published (Thiele et al., 2013; Mardinoglu et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites recent publications of comprehensive human metabolic models.

claim: Generic human metabolic models have successfully served as a basis for generating context-specific models of tissues.
source: While these generic models are not specific to any cell- or tissue-type, they have successfully served both as a basis for generating context-specific models of tissues (Shlomi et al., 2008; Jerby et al., 2010; Agren et al., 2012) and for studying cancer metabolism (Folger et al., 2011; Frezza et al., 2011; Shlomi et al., 2011; Agren et al., 2012; Facchetti et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012; Dolfi et al., 2013; Agren et al., 2014; Yizhak et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple studies demonstrating the use of generic models for context-specific modeling.

claim: Methods for building context-specific models do not take into account subtle differences in levels of expression of a particular enzyme.
source: Importantly, methods for building context-specific models do not take into account subtle differences in levels of expression of a particular enzyme, but rather its presence or absence.
evidence: The introduction describes a limitation of existing context-specific modeling methods.

claim: Coarse discretization of expression data makes existing methods less applicable for building cell-specific models when inter-individual variations are small.
source: This coarse discretization makes these methods less applicable for the task of building cell-specific models, in cases where a high similarity in transcriptomics levels of different samples is observed.
evidence: The introduction explains why existing methods are limited for cell-specific modeling with similar samples.

claim: E-Flux uses absolute expression levels to constraint the model's solution space.
source: Alternatively, absolute expression levels can be used to constraint the model's solution space, as previously done by E-Flux for studying bacterial metabolism (Colijn et al., 2009).
evidence: The introduction cites E-Flux as a method using absolute expression levels.

claim: The applicability of E-Flux for studying human metabolism has not been established.
source: Nonetheless, the applicability of E-Flux for studying human metabolism has not been established.
evidence: The introduction states a gap in knowledge regarding E-Flux application to human metabolism.

claim: The difference in gene expression between HapMap and NCI-60 datasets is very subtle with mean Spearman R > 0.92.
source: The difference in the gene expression of HapMap and NCI-60 datasets is very subtle (mean Spearman R > 0.92, Figure 1A, upper panel)
evidence: The results section presents correlation data showing high similarity in gene expression between samples.

claim: iMAT resulted in insignificant or negative correlations between actual and predicted proliferation rates for both HapMap and NCI-60 datasets.
source: iMAT, an omics-integration method that defines a subset of active and inactive reactions based on expression data (Shlomi et al., 2008), resulted in insignificant or even negative correlations between the actual and predicted proliferation rates for both datasets (HapMap: Spearman R = 0.03, p-value = 0.66; NCI-60: Spearman R = −0.07, p-value = 0.59, Figure 1A middle panel, Figure 2A)
evidence: The results section presents specific correlation values and p-values for iMAT predictions.

claim: E-flux failed to obtain significant results in predicting the HapMap cell lines' proliferation rates.
source: E-flux (Colijn et al., 2009) similarly failed to obtain significant results in predicting the HapMap cell lines' proliferation rates (Spearman R in the range of 0.1–0.11, p-value > 0.07, Figure 1A lower panel, Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1A)
evidence: The results section presents specific correlation values and p-values for E-flux predictions on HapMap data.

claim: E-flux obtained significant results in predicting the NCI-60 cell lines' proliferation rate.
source: but obtained significant results in predicting the NCI-60 cell lines' proliferation rate (Spearman R in the range of 0.43–0.44, p-value > 3.6e-4, Figure 1A lower panel, Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The results section presents specific correlation values and p-values for E-flux predictions on NCI-60 data.

claim: PRIME identifies a set of genes significantly correlated with the key phenotype of interest.
source: (1) A set of genes that are significantly correlated with the key phenotype of interest is determined (Supplementary file 2A);
evidence: The results section describes the first step of the PRIME algorithm.

claim: PRIME modifies the maximal flux capacity of reactions according to the directionality and level of their corresponding gene expression.
source: (2) The maximal flux capacity of reactions associated with the genes identified in (1) is modified according to the directionality and level of their corresponding gene expression level.
evidence: The results section describes the second step of the PRIME algorithm.

claim: PRIME modifies reactions' flux bounds within an effective flux range to ensure modifications affect the models' solution space.
source: Importantly, to assure that bound modifications would have an effect on the models' solution space, reactions' flux bounds are modified within an effective flux range.
evidence: The results section explains a key feature of PRIME's methodology.

claim: 224 metabolic models were constructed for lymphoblast cell lines from the HapMap project using PRIME.
source: We first applied PRIME to a dataset composed of 224 lymphoblast cell lines from the HapMap project (International HapMap Consortium, 2005). This dataset is composed of cell lines taken from healthy human individuals, from four different populations, including Caucasian (CEU), African (YRI), Chinese (CHB) and Japanese (JPT) ethnicities (Supplementary file 1B). Applying PRIME to the generic human model (Duarte et al., 2007), we constructed the corresponding 224 metabolic models, one for each cell line.
evidence: The results section describes the application of PRIME to HapMap data.

claim: The correlation between proliferation rates predicted by PRIME models and those measured experimentally for HapMap cell lines is highly significant (Spearman R = 0.44, p-value = 5.87e-12).
source: The correlation between the proliferation rates predicted by these models and those measured experimentally is highly significant (Spearman R = 0.44, p-value = 5.87e-12, Figure 2A–B, Supplementary file 1C and Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: The results section presents specific correlation values and p-values for PRIME predictions on HapMap data.

claim: PRIME models correctly predict the experimentally observed significant differences between HapMap populations' proliferation rates in the correct order (CEU < YRI < JPT < CHB).
source: In addition to capturing the differences between each of the cell lines the models also correctly predict the experimentally observed significant differences between populations' proliferation rates (CEU < YRI < JPT < CHB) in the correct order (Figure 2C and [Stark et al., 2010]).
evidence: The results section describes PRIME's ability to predict population-level differences with citation support.

claim: Five-fold cross validation of PRIME on HapMap data resulted in a mean Spearman R = 0.26 with empiric p-value = 0.007.
source: The correlation observed remains significant also after employing a five-fold cross validation process 1000 times, controlling for the (indirect) use of proliferation rate in determining the modified reactions' set (mean Spearman R = 0.26, empiric p-value = 0.007, Figure 2A, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The results section presents cross-validation results for PRIME on HapMap data.

claim: PRIME applied to NCI-60 cancer cell lines obtained a highly significant correlation between measured and predicted proliferation rates (Spearman R = 0.69, p-value = 1.22e-9).
source: We further applied PRIME to build individual models and predict the proliferation rates of 60 cancer cell lines, obtaining a highly significant correlation between the measured and predicted proliferation rates (Spearman R = 0.69, p-value = 1.22e-9, Figure 2A–B, Supplementary file 1C and Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: The results section presents specific correlation values and p-values for PRIME predictions on NCI-60 data.

claim: Four-fold cross-validation of PRIME on NCI-60 data resulted in a mean Spearman correlation of 0.56 with empiric p-value = 0.006.
source: A four-fold cross-validation analysis resulted with a mean Spearman correlation of 0.56 (empiric p-value = 0.006, Figure 2A, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The results section presents cross-validation results for PRIME on NCI-60 data.

claim: A significant correlation is obtained between the measured and actual growth rates of different tumor types in the NCI-60 dataset (Spearman R = 0.71, p-value = 0.03).
source: Grouping the samples into the nine tumor types found in this dataset and evaluating the mean proliferation rate of each group, a significant correlation is obtained between the measured and actual growth rates of the different tumors (Spearman R = 0.71, p-value = 0.03, Figure 2D).
evidence: The results section presents correlation data for tumor type-specific predictions.

claim: The higher correlation achieved for cancer cell-lines compared to normal cell-lines is a result of higher correlation between metabolic gene expression and growth rate in the cancer dataset.
source: The higher correlation achieved for the cancer cell-lines in respect to that achieved for the normal cell-lines, is a result of the higher correlation found between metabolic gene expression and growth rate in the former datatset (see Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: The results section provides an explanation for the difference in performance between datasets.

claim: Modifying the bounds of all enzyme-associated reactions instead of only growth-related ones decreased the correlation for both NCI-60 and HapMap datasets.
source: To further examine the process employed by PRIME we tested three additional alternatives: (1) modifying the bounds of all enzyme-associated reactions and not only of those that are growth-related. This process decreased the correlation to Spearman R = 0.24, p-value = 2.4e-9 and Spearman R = 0.56, p-value = 2.8e-6 for the NCI-60 and HapMap datasets, respectively;
evidence: The results section presents data from alternative approaches to validate PRIME's methodology.

claim: Selecting random sets of reactions resulted in significantly inferior predictive performance compared to PRIME in both datasets (empiric p-value < 9.9e-4).
source: (2) selecting random sets of reactions at the size of the original set and modifying their bounds according to their gene expression. Repeating this process 1000 times resulted with significantly inferior predictive performance in both datasets compared to PRIME (empiric p-value < 9.9e-4, 'Materials and methods');
evidence: The results section presents permutation test results validating PRIME's approach.

claim: Permuting measured proliferation rates 1000 times showed that original growth prediction results were highly superior (empiric p-value < 9.9e-4).
source: (3) permuting the measured proliferation rates in each of the cell lines datasets for a 1000 times and correlating them with those computed by the PRIME models. In this case as well the original growth prediction results were found to be highly superior (empiric p-value < 9.9e-4, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The results section presents permutation test results validating PRIME's predictions.

claim: PRIME achieved significant Spearman correlation (p-value < 0.05) between measured and predicted drug response for 12 out of 16 drugs tested.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, this analysis yields a significant Spearman correlation (p-value < 0.05) between measured and predicted drug response for 12 out of 16 drugs tested in the HapMap and the NCI-60 datasets.
evidence: The results section presents drug response prediction data.

claim: Permutation test on measured drug response data yielded highly significant results (empiric p-value < 9.9e-4).
source: Moreover, performing a permutation test in each of the datasets separately by permuting the measured drug response data, a highly significant result is obtained (empiric p-value < 9.9e-4, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The results section presents permutation test results for drug response predictions.

claim: Partial correlation analysis between predicted and measured drug response while controlling for proliferation rate showed significant association for HapMap and CEU datasets.
source: Applying a partial correlation analysis between in silico predicted and measured drug response while controlling for the experimentally measured proliferation rate (as growth rate itself has been implicated as a predictor of drug response, e.g., for cytotoxic drugs), we still find a significant association between predicted and measured drug response for the HapMap and CEU datasets, and in some cases even higher than before (Supplementary file 1D–E).
evidence: The results section presents partial correlation analysis results.

claim: Significant correlations between measured and predicted uptake and secretion rates were obtained for 14 out of 33 metabolites.
source: We obtained significant Spearman correlations (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value with False Discovery Rate (FDR) and α = 0.05) for 14 out of 33 metabolites with a corresponding transporter reaction in the human model (Figure 3B).
evidence: The results section presents metabolite uptake/secretion prediction data.

claim: Permutation test on measured uptake and secretion data yielded highly significant results (empiric p-value < 9.9e-4).
source: By performing a permutation test on the measured data a highly significant result is obtained (empiric p-value < 9.9e-4, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The results section presents permutation test results for metabolite flux predictions.

claim: E-Flux models yielded insignificant results for all metabolites when predicting uptake and secretion rates.
source: Importantly, utilizing the models reconstructed by E-Flux for the same task, insignificant results are obtained for all metabolites.
evidence: The results section compares PRIME performance to E-Flux for metabolite flux predictions.

claim: The set of predicted non-selective targets was highly enriched with current cytostatic drugs (mean hypergeometric p-value = 7.28e-4).
source: The set of predicted non-selective targets was highly enriched with current cytostatic drugs (Wishart et al., 2008; Folger et al., 2011) (mean hypergeometric p-value = 7.28e-4, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: The results section presents enrichment analysis of predicted non-selective targets.

claim: Three out of five metabolic enzyme drug targets reported by Cheong et al. were identified as selective by PRIME (Hypergeometric p-value = 3.98e-4).
source: Second, the predicted selective targets were enriched with targets of newly developed drugs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1): Out of the five metabolic enzyme drug targets reported in (Cheong et al., 2012), our analysis identified three as being selective (Hypergeometric p-value = 3.98e-4; Supplementary file 2C).
evidence: The results section presents enrichment analysis of predicted selective targets with citation.

claim: Predicted selective targets are enriched with genes whose lower expression is significantly associated with improved survival in breast cancer patients (Hypergeometric p-value = 2.1e-5).
source: A Cox multivariate regression analysis shows that this set is enriched (Hypergeometric p-value = 2.1e-5) with genes whose lower expression is significantly associated with improved survival (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values with FDR and α = 0.1, 'Materials and methods'), when examined together with known prognostic variables such as patients' clinical stage, histological grade, tumor size, lymph node status and estrogen receptor status.
evidence: The results section presents survival analysis results for predicted selective targets.

claim: MLYCD is a top predicted selective target.
source: A top predicted selective target is Malonyl-CoA Decarboxylase (MLYCD) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The results section identifies MLYCD as a top prediction.

claim: E-Flux predicts that MLYCD knock down reduces both normal and cancer cell proliferation by less than 10%.
source: Of note, the knock down of MLYCD is predicted by E-Flux to reduce both normal and cancer cell proliferation by less than 10%, suggesting that without including phenotype-based constraints, this candidate gene would have not been revealed (Figure 3D).
evidence: The results section compares PRIME and E-Flux predictions for MLYCD.

claim: MLYCD has been recently proposed as potential anticancer target for breast cancer.
source: Interestingly, this enzyme has been recently proposed as potential anticancer target for breast cancer (Zhou et al., 2009), however its selective effects on other tumor types have not been assessed.
evidence: The results section cites prior work on MLYCD as a cancer target.

claim: siRNA-mediated silencing of MLYCD significantly inhibited the proliferation of leukemia cell lines RPMI-8226 and K562 cells.
source: In line with PRIME's predictions, the small interfering RNA (siRNA)-mediated silencing of MLYCD significantly inhibited the proliferation of the leukemia cell lines RPMI-8226 and K562 cells, but had no effect on HapMap cells (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: The results section presents experimental validation data for MLYCD knockdown in leukemia cells.

claim: siRNA-mediated silencing of MLYCD had no effect on HapMap cells.
source: In line with PRIME's predictions, the small interfering RNA (siRNA)-mediated silencing of MLYCD significantly inhibited the proliferation of the leukemia cell lines RPMI-8226 and K562 cells, but had no effect on HapMap cells (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: The results section presents experimental validation data showing selectivity of MLYCD knockdown.

claim: Silencing of MLYCD suppressed proliferation of renal cancer cell lines TK-10 and CAKI-1 without affecting the non-transformed renal cell line HK-2.
source: Of note, the silencing of MLYCD suppressed proliferation of renal cancer cell lines without affecting the non-transformed counterpart (Figure 4D).
evidence: The results section presents experimental validation data for MLYCD knockdown in renal cells.

claim: The anti-proliferative effects of MLYCD suppression could not be explained by different expression of the enzyme among different cell lines.
source: Importantly, the anti-proliferative effects of MLYCD suppression could not be explained by the different expression of the enzyme among the different cell lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section presents data ruling out expression level as explanation for selectivity.

claim: MLYCD depletion leads to the accumulation of malonyl-CoA, which blocks fatty acid oxidation by allosteric inhibition of CPT1.
source: Previous reports have shown that MLYCD depletion leads to the accumulation of malonyl-CoA, which blocks fatty acid oxidation by allosteric inhibition of the mitochondrial enzyme Carnitine-Palmitoyl-Transferase (CPT1) (Zhou et al., 2009).
evidence: The results section cites prior work on the mechanism of MLYCD depletion.

claim: A significant decrease in 13C-labelling of palmitoyl-carnitine was observed in MLYCD-depleted cells.
source: We observed a significant decrease in the 13C-labelling of palmitoyl-carnitine (Figure 5B) and of the m+2 isotopologues of TCA cycle intermediates (Figure 5C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3 for the full isotopologue analyses of these metabolites), indicating that fatty acid oxidation is reduced in MLYCD-depleted cells.
evidence: The results section presents isotope tracing data showing reduced fatty acid oxidation.

claim: A significant decrease in m+2 isotopologues of TCA cycle intermediates was observed in MLYCD-depleted cells.
source: We observed a significant decrease in the 13C-labelling of palmitoyl-carnitine (Figure 5B) and of the m+2 isotopologues of TCA cycle intermediates (Figure 5C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3 for the full isotopologue analyses of these metabolites), indicating that fatty acid oxidation is reduced in MLYCD-depleted cells.
evidence: The results section presents isotope tracing data showing altered TCA cycle metabolism.

claim: Fatty acid oxidation is reduced in MLYCD-depleted cells.
source: We observed a significant decrease in the 13C-labelling of palmitoyl-carnitine (Figure 5B) and of the m+2 isotopologues of TCA cycle intermediates (Figure 5C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3 for the full isotopologue analyses of these metabolites), indicating that fatty acid oxidation is reduced in MLYCD-depleted cells.
evidence: The results section interprets isotope tracing data as evidence of reduced fatty acid oxidation.

claim: A striking accumulation of succinate and a decrease in fumarate and malate were observed in MLYCD-depleted cells.
source: We also noticed a striking accumulation of succinate and a decrease in fumarate and malate in MLYCD-depleted cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The results section presents metabolite abundance data.

claim: The accumulation of succinate and decrease in fumarate and malate are consistent with inhibition of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH).
source: These results are consistent with the inhibition of the TCA cycle enzyme succinate dehydrogenase (SDH), which may be caused by malonyl-CoA-derived malonate.
evidence: The results section interprets metabolite data as consistent with SDH inhibition.

claim: PRIME-derived models predict that upon MLYCD suppression, part of the accumulated malonyl-CoA is diverted to fatty acid biosynthesis.
source: Of note, the model predicted that upon MLYCD suppression, part of the accumulated malonyl-CoA is diverted to fatty acid biosynthesis.
evidence: The results section presents a prediction from PRIME models.

claim: The m+4 and m+6 isotopologues of palmitate were significantly increased in MLYCD-depleted cells.
source: While the labeling of citrate, the main lipogenic precursor, was, if any, slightly decreased (Figure 5E), the m+4 and m+6 isotopologues of palmitate were significantly increased in MLYCD-depleted cells (Figure 5F), suggesting that fatty acid synthesis is accelerated in these cells.
evidence: The results section presents isotope tracing data showing increased fatty acid synthesis.

claim: Fatty acid synthesis is accelerated in MLYCD-depleted cells.
source: While the labeling of citrate, the main lipogenic precursor, was, if any, slightly decreased (Figure 5E), the m+4 and m+6 isotopologues of palmitate were significantly increased in MLYCD-depleted cells (Figure 5F), suggesting that fatty acid synthesis is accelerated in these cells.
evidence: The results section interprets isotope tracing data as evidence of accelerated fatty acid synthesis.

claim: PPP flux was increased in MLYCD-depleted cells.
source: As predicted by PRIME, PPP flux was increased in MLYCD-depleted cells (Figure 5H–I).
evidence: The results section presents isotope tracing data showing increased pentose phosphate pathway activity.

claim: MLYCD-depleted cells exhibited a lower GSH/GSSG ratio compared to control cells.
source: In line with this hypothesis, MLYCD-depleted cells exhibited a lower GSH/GSSG ratio compared to control cells (Figure 5I).
evidence: The results section presents data showing altered redox homeostasis.

claim: Incubation with N-acetyl-cysteine (NAC) fully restored the proliferation defects observed in MLYCD-depleted cells.
source: Furthermore, the incubation of cells with the antioxidant N-acetyl-cysteine (NAC) fully restored the proliferation defects observed in MLYCD-depleted cells (Figure 5J).
evidence: The results section presents experimental data showing rescue of proliferation defects by antioxidant.

claim: The suppression of cancer cell proliferation caused by loss of MLYCD depends, at least in part, on aberrant activation of fatty acid synthesis leading to reduced ability to maintain redox homeostasis.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the suppression of cancer cell proliferation caused by the loss of MLYCD depends, at least in part, on the aberrant activation of fatty acid synthesis, which leads to a reduced ability of cells to maintain redox homeostasis.
evidence: The results section synthesizes multiple experimental findings into a mechanistic conclusion.

claim: 11 out of 13 genes tested were found to have an effect on cell growth as predicted by PRIME models.
source: 11 out of the 13 genes studied were found to have an effect on cell growth as predicted by the models (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 2D, empiric p-value < 0.01, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The results section presents experimental validation data for predicted differential effects.

claim: A significant correlation is obtained between predicted and measured % inhibition values across all 11 validated targets (Spearman R = 0.64, p-value = 1e-3).
source: A significant correlation is obtained between predicted and measured % inhibition values across all 11 targets (Spearman R = 0.64, p-value = 1e-3).
evidence: The results section presents correlation data for experimental validation of predictions.

claim: Patients with predicted low growth rate had significantly improved survival compared to those with predicted high growth rate in breast cancer datasets (logrank p-values: 0.01 and 1e-3).
source: A Kaplan–Meier survival analysis (Kaplan and Meier, 1958) showed that patients with predicted low growth rate had significantly improved survival compared to those with a predicted high growth rate (logrank p-values are: 0.01, 1e-3 and 0.02 for Miller et al., Chang et al. and Okayama et al. respectively, Figure 6B, Supplementary file 1I, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The results section presents survival analysis data for patient models.

claim: Patients with predicted low growth rate had significantly improved survival compared to those with predicted high growth rate in lung cancer dataset (logrank p-value: 0.02).
source: A Kaplan–Meier survival analysis (Kaplan and Meier, 1958) showed that patients with predicted low growth rate had significantly improved survival compared to those with a predicted high growth rate (logrank p-values are: 0.01, 1e-3 and 0.02 for Miller et al., Chang et al. and Okayama et al. respectively, Figure 6B, Supplementary file 1I, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The results section presents survival analysis data for patient models.

claim: Cox univariate survival analysis supported the association between predicted growth rate and survival (p-values: 1e-3, 1e-4, and 2e-3 for the three datasets).
source: This result was further supported by a Cox univariate survival analysis (Grambsch, 2000) (p-values are: 1e-3, 1e-4 and 2e-3 for Miller et al., Chang et al. and Okayama et al. respectively, Supplementary file 1I)
evidence: The results section presents Cox regression analysis results.

claim: Estimating samples' growth rates directly from gene expression data using multiple linear regression resulted in inferior performance compared to PRIME.
source: Of note, estimating the samples growth rates directly from the gene expression data by using multiple linear regression, resulted in inferior performance (Supplementary file 1J), testifying to the added value of personalized GSMMs.
evidence: The results section compares PRIME to an alternative approach.

claim: iMAT and E-Flux fail to obtain meaningful and significant results when applied to patient survival prediction.
source: Importantly, while iMAT and E-Flux require only 'omics' data and can hence be applied directly, they fail to obtain meaningful and significant results in this setting as well (Supplementary file 1K).
evidence: The results section compares PRIME to existing methods for patient modeling.

claim: PRIME is the first method able to generate human cell-specific GSMMs that can predict metabolic phenotypes in an individual manner.
source: To the best of our knowledge, PRIME is the first method able to generate human cell-specific GSMMs that can predict metabolic phenotypes in an individual manner, including growth rates and drug response.
evidence: The discussion claims novelty of PRIME based on the results presented.

claim: PRIME assumes that cells try to maximize their proliferation.
source: First, PRIME assumes that cells try to maximize their proliferation, while different objective function(s) should be considered for non-proliferating cells.
evidence: The discussion explicitly states an assumption of PRIME.

claim: PRIME assumes that all models share the same set of enzymes and differ only in their cellular abundance.
source: Second, we assume that all models share the same set of enzymes and differ only in their cellular abundance, but different cells may express different coding variants that should be incorporated in future studies.
evidence: The discussion explicitly states an assumption and limitation of PRIME.

claim: PRIME relies on the measurement of a specific phenotype that is not always available for a given set of cells or samples.
source: Third, PRIME relies on the measurement of a specific phenotype that is not always available for a given set of cells or samples.
evidence: The discussion explicitly states a limitation of PRIME.

claim: The silencing of MLYCD has an anti-proliferative effect across multiple cancer cell lines but spares non-transformed counterparts.
source: Our results show that the silencing of MLYCD has an anti-proliferative effect across multiple cancer cell lines but spares the non-transformed counterparts, confirming PRIME's predictions.
evidence: The discussion summarizes experimental validation results.

claim: In humans, the loss of MLYCD leads to methylmalonic aciduria, an extremely rare autosomal recessive disorder.
source: Importantly, in humans, the loss of MLYCD leads to methylmalonic aciduria, an extremely rare autosomal recessive disorder.
evidence: The discussion states a known clinical consequence of MLYCD deficiency.

claim: In vivo experiments in rodents and pigs, ex vivo experiments in human skeletal muscle, and experiments in MRC-5 non-transformed fibroblasts suggest that inhibition of MLYCD is well tolerated.
source: Nevertheless, in vivo experiments in rodents and pigs (Dyck et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2014), ex vivo experiments in human skeletal muscle (Bouzakri et al., 2008), and in MRC-5 non-transformed fibroblasts (Zhou et al., 2009) suggest that the inhibition of MLYCD is well tolerated, as our results indicate.
evidence: The discussion cites multiple studies supporting tolerability of MLYCD inhibition.

claim: Incorporating gene expression measurements and phenotypic data within a genome-scale model of human metabolism via PRIME results in functional cell-specific models with considerable predictive power.
source: In summary, we here show that incorporating gene expression measurements and phenotypic data within a genome-scale model of human metabolism via PRIME results in functional cell-specific models with considerable predictive power.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the main conclusion based on the results presented.

claim: A metabolic network consisting of m metabolites and n reactions can be represented by a stoichiometric matrix S.
source: A metabolic network consisting of m metabolites and n reactions can be represented by a stoichiometric matrix S, where the entry Sij represents the stoichiometric coefficient of metabolite i in reaction j (Price et al., 2004).
evidence: The methods section describes the mathematical representation of metabolic networks with citation.

claim: The steady-state assumption constrains the production rate of each metabolite to be equal to its consumption rate.
source: The steady-state assumption represented in Equation (1) constrains the production rate of each metabolite to be equal to its consumption rate.
evidence: The methods section explains the steady-state assumption in metabolic modeling.

claim: The biomass function utilized is taken from Folger et al., 2011.
source: The biomass function utilized here is taken from (Folger et al., 2011).
evidence: The methods section cites the source of the biomass function used.

claim: The media simulated in all analyses is the RPMI-1640 media.
source: The media simulated in all the analyses throughout the paper is the RPMI-1640 media that was used to grow the cell lines experimentally (Lee et al., 2007; Choy et al., 2008).
evidence: The methods section specifies the growth media used in simulations with citations.

claim: Gene knock outs are simulated by constraining the flux through the corresponding metabolic reaction to zero.
source: Gene knock outs are simulated by constraining the flux through the corresponding metabolic reaction to zero.
evidence: The methods section describes how gene knockouts are simulated in the models.

claim: Expression data and growth rate measurements for the HapMap dataset were taken from Choy et al., 2008.
source: Expression data and growth rate measurements for the HapMap dataset were taken from (Choy et al., 2008).
